verses.text: Elisha said, “Hear Yahweh’s word. Yahweh says, ‘Tomorrow about this time a seah  of fine flour will be sold for a shekel,  and two seahs of barley for a shekel, in the gate of Samaria.’”

Then the captain on whose hand the king leaned answered the man of God, and said, “Behold, if Yahweh made windows in heaven, could this thing be?” He said, “Behold, you will see it with your eyes, but will not eat of it.”
Now there were four leprous men at the entrance of the gate. They said to one another, “Why do we sit here until we die?

If we say, ‘We will enter into the city,’ then the famine is in the city, and we will die there. If we sit still here, we also die. Now therefore come, and let us surrender to the army of the Syrians. If they save us alive, we will live; and if they kill us, we will only die.”
They rose up in the twilight, to go to the camp of the Syrians. When they had come to the outermost part of the camp of the Syrians, behold, no man was there.

For the Lord  had made the army of the Syrians to hear the sound of chariots, and the sound of horses, even the noise of a great army; and they said to one another, “Behold, the king of Israel has hired against us the kings of the Hittites and the kings of the Egyptians to attack us.”
Therefore they arose and fled in the twilight, and left their tents, and their horses, and their donkeys, even the camp as it was, and fled for their life.

When these lepers came to the outermost part of the camp, they went into one tent, and ate and drink, and carried away silver, gold, and clothing, and went and hid it. Then they came back, and entered into another tent, and carried things from there also, and went and hid them.

Then they said to one another, “We aren’t doing right. Today is a day of good news, and we keep silent. If we wait until the morning light, punishment will overtake us. Now therefore come, let’s go and tell the king’s household.”

So they came and called to the city gatekeepers; and they told them, “We came to the camp of the Syrians, and, behold, there was no man there, not even a man’s voice, but the horses tied, and the donkeys tied, and the tents as they were.”
He called the gatekeepers; and they told it to the king’s household within.

The king arose in the night, and said to his servants, “I will now show you what the Syrians have done to us. They know that we are hungry. Therefore are they gone out of the camp to hide themselves in the field, saying, ‘When they come out of the city, we shall take them alive, and get into the city.’”

One of his servants answered, “Please let some people take five of the horses that remain, which are left in the city. Behold, they are like all the multitude of Israel who are left in it. Behold, they are like all the multitude of Israel who are consumed. Let us send and see.”
Therefore they took two chariots with horses; and the king them sent out to the Syrian army, saying, “Go and see.”
They went after them to the Jordan; and behold, all the path was full of garments and equipment which the Syrians had cast away in their haste. The messengers returned, and told the king.
The people went out and plundered the camp of the Syrians. So a seah  of fine flour was sold for a shekel, and two measures of barley for a shekel,  according to Yahweh’s word.

The king appointed the captain on whose hand he leaned to be in charge of the gate; and the people trampled over him in the gate, and he died as the man of God had said, who spoke when the king came down to him.
It happened as the man of God had spoken to the king, saying, “Two seahs  of barley for a shekel,  and a seah of fine flour for a shekel, shall be tomorrow about this time in the gate of Samaria”;

and that captain answered the man of God, and said, “Now, behold, if Yahweh made windows in heaven, might such a thing be?” and he said, “Behold, you will see it with your eyes, but will not eat of it.”
It happened like that to him; for the people trampled over him in the gate, and he died.

footnotes.content: Elisha speaks with such certainty—'Tomorrow about this time'—when Samaria is starving behind siege walls. He doesn't argue or defend; he simply declares what the Lord says will come to pass. That quiet confidence in a whispered promise is what faith looks like when the situation seems impossible.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The captain's sneer—'if Yahweh made windows in heaven'—is a taunt wrapped in sarcasm. Yet Elisha doesn't curse him; he simply says, 'You will see it with your eyes, but will not eat of it.' Unbelief meets truth, and the judgment follows the refusal, not anger. The Lord lets our doubt speak for itself.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Four leprous men sit outside the gate—utterly alone, cast out from the city, dying of hunger and disease both. Their question, 'Why do we sit here until we die?' comes from the deepest helplessness. And yet the Lord is about to use these four forgotten souls to save an entire city.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Listen to their logic: every path leads to death—the city brings starvation, staying here brings slow death, and surrender might bring death too. So they choose surrender not from hope, but from the clarity that at least they're choosing. Sometimes the Lord moves in those moments when we stop trying to avoid dying and simply move toward something, anything else.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They rise at twilight and walk toward the enemy camp. No one told them to go; the king didn't send them. They simply moved—four untouchable, desperate men walking into the dark, toward what should have been their destruction. And the camp was empty. God had already cleared the way before they ever took the first step.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Lord made the Syrian army hear phantom sounds—chariots, horses, a great army rushing in. They panicked and fled without a shot fired. How often does He deliver us not by a show of force but by mastering the fear inside our enemies' hearts? The battle was won in their minds before they ever turned to run.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: In their haste, they left everything—tents, horses, donkeys. Not a single thing gathered. The Lord didn't just save His people; He left their persecutors' camp fully stocked, as if He'd prepared a feast. Deliverance came with abundance, not bare survival. Our God is generous in His rescues.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The lepers enter the tent and eat their fill—probably the first real meal any of them had had in weeks. Then they hoard silver, gold, clothes, hide them away. For a moment, fear grips them: treasure and survival are precious when you've had nothing. But hoarding passes, and conscience stirs.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: 'Today is a day of good news, and we keep silent.' They pause mid-plunder and remember: a city is starving while they feast in secret. Grace wakes them up. They realize that keeping good news to themselves turns joy into guilt, and they choose to share the news that will save their people, even though telling the king means giving up their advantage.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They come to the city gate and report plainly: no man there, just animals tied and tents standing. Their testimony is simple, urgent, true. Four outcasts become the bearers of the city's deliverance—not generals, not kings, just four lepers who chose to tell what they'd seen.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The gatekeepers pass the word up through the household to the king himself. The message travels from the margin to the throne—from those who have always been outside, to those who rule. Sometimes the Lord speaks through the ones we've forgotten to listen to.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The king, waking at night, suspects a trap: 'They've gone to hide and will ambush us when we leave the city.' His fear is reasonable—he's leading from scarcity and mistrust. He reads mercy as deception because he's forgotten that the Lord defends His people without their scheming. Fear whispers conspiracy even when deliverance stands at the door.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A servant offers a practical suggestion: send scouts with a few horses to verify. He's wise to say, 'What have we got to lose?'—the city's dying anyway. When desperation meets a glimmer of hope, sometimes a simple yes to one small step is all faith needs to begin.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Two chariots with horses—that's all the king can spare—go out to scout. A tiny probe into the dark, risking a handful of soldiers and animals to check whether the lepers told the truth. Sending scouts is the city's first small obedience, and obedience is where deliverance always begins.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The road to the Jordan is strewn with garments and equipment the Syrians threw down in their panic. It's a mile-long trail of proof—every piece a witness that the Lord has truly scattered the enemy. The path itself becomes testimony, and the messengers race back with joy.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The people rush out and plunder the camp—and the prophecy is fulfilled exactly as Elisha spoke it. Bread becomes cheap again. Famine turns to plenty in a single day. The Lord keeps His word with such precision that we can set our watches by it. He never exaggerates or fails by a hair's breadth.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The very captain who mocked Elisha—'if Yahweh made windows in heaven'—is trampled to death in the gate by the very crowd rushing to eat the abundance he doubted. He saw it with his eyes, but never ate of it, exactly as the prophet said. His fate stands as a quiet warning: unbelief shapes its own judgment.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The writer pauses to rehearse Elisha's exact words again: two seahs of barley, a seah of fine flour, all for a shekel, 'tomorrow about this time.' By repeating it, he underlines the marvel—not metaphor, not approximate, but fulfilled down to the measure and the hour. The Lord speaks like an architect, and His word follows the blueprint.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The captain's mockery is replayed for us once more: 'If Yahweh made windows in heaven, might such a thing be?' His taunt was the last word he heard before stepping into the gate. Unbelief doesn't win arguments; it simply stands aside while grace moves in and does what seemed impossible. His disbelief made no dent in God's purpose.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Readers today hear an echo in that captain's trampling death: we reap what we've sown in unbelief, not in cruelty from God, but as the natural harvest of doubt standing unmoved when grace pours out all around. Looking back, I see how often those who refuse to trust miss the very abundance meant for them, while those with open hands receive everything.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
